messages.subject: Aerial survey question
messages.body_plain:
Dear Listserve,

We conducted an aerial survey on white-tailed deer and estimated the
population using distance sampling methods.  The surveys were conducted
from a fixed-wing plane flown at 200 meters.  We used 8 transects, flown
east to west, varying in length from 27.5 to 32.0 km.  Each transect was
repeated 6 times due to the small sample size we were observing per
flight.  Distances were estimated in bins 0-50 meters, 50-100, etc. with
the last distance as 250+ which is placed in a 250-300 meter bin.   We
followed the directions in the User Guide (Ch 8, pg. 98-99) and used the
midpoint (e.g. 25 meters for the 0-50 m bin) as the distance for each
observation.  In the analysis stage we turned the data into intervals
using the Intervals tab of the Data Filter.  We pooled all the data from
each transect into one effort.  The total effort was 1431 km, 150
observations and 226 deer.  The density estimate came to 1.20 deer/mi2,
which is very low, even for this area.  The histogram showed less than
expected on the first bin, indicating either that deer were missed or
that deer flushed and moved off the transect.   I tried to attach a
picture of the histogram, but the email was rejected.  However, the
detection probability was about 0.41 in the first bin, followed by 1.38
next bin and then decreasing.  What do you recommend to do at this point
from an analysis standpoint?  The most likely explanation is that deer
are missed on the line.  However, the doesn't explain the peak in the
50-100 meter bin - if deer were missed due to habitat obstruction, then
wouldn't they be missed equally on the next bin? If deer were missed due
to the obstruction by the plane, should we subtract that distance from
all the distances and effectively move the line away from the center
line?  Any advice you can give would be greatly appreciated.  Thank you.

   =20

messages.subject: Re: Aerial survey question
messages.body_plain:
Elina-

You may want to refer to pgs 284-287 of the Intro to Distance Sampling.
Also, you need to provide some more details. From what you described it
isn't possible to tell whether the observers could see directly below
the aircraft.   Did the plane have bubble windows or flat windows?  Or
was there a belly window for downward visibility?  Or was the line
offset such that 0 is really something like 72 m from the line?  If the
plane has flat windows, it is my experience that the observer can only
see down to a 70 degree angle from the horizon at best.  At a 200 m
flight altitude that is 72 m from the line.  Also, from my experience
observers prefer not to look straight down  as it is not comfortable on
the neck and it can make some people airsick.  So the tendency is to
look at more like a 50-60 degree angle down from the horizon.  Because
there focus is further away from the line they tend to miss the animals
closer to the line.  I think that is a more likely explanation for the
histogram.  You may also want to consider some of the subjects described
in the following article.  I'll send a pdf separately to you.

LAAKE, J., R. J. GUENZEL, J. L. BENGTSON, P. BOVENG, M. CAMERON and M.
B. HANSON. 2008. Coping with variation in aerial survey protocol for
line-transect sampling. Wildlife Research 35: 289-298.

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Re: adjust how distances are collected at close distances?
messages.subject_clean: adjust how distances are collected at close distances?
messages.body_plain:
Kim, I think your reference to the distance sampling book is to the 1993
book.  The 2001 book has more relevant comments on this topic - but in
any case, you have misunderstood what is said on p307.  It says that, by
spending some time at the point, it increases the chances of detecting
all birds close to the point.  It does NOT say that most detected birds
will be very close to the point - in fact, quite the reverse is
expected, as the area within say 5m of the point is very small, so tends
to hold very few birds.  If you're getting lots of detections within 5m
of the point, then I suspect you have problems with assumptions.  It's
possible that you're dealing with birds that for the most part aren't
detectable unless they're very close - in which case it would be better
to measure exact distances as far as possible.  However, 10-min counts
are unlikely to work well if this is the case.  Suppose for example that
you have a bird that isn't detectable unless it is within 5m of the
point.  Suppose also that it is moving around during the 10-min count.
By waiting for 10-mins, you're increasing the chance that the bird will
move to within 5m of the point.  So that is where you detect it.  This
is systematically reducing detection distances, and would lead to
overestimation of density.  Distance sampling is a snapshot method.
I'll send you separately a pdf of a paper of mine on this issue that
appeared in 2006 in the Auk.  It explains why conventional methods can
be expected to overestimate density for species that typically move
around, and how methods can be made to work.

If you're dealing with songbirds, with surveys conducted in the breeding
season, you may want to consider surveying singing males only, as these
are much more detectable, allowing estimation with low bias and high
precision.  This may force an assumption that there is on average one
female for every male, and for some species, it may be necessary to
estimate the proportion of males that can be expected to sing within a
given time interval.  If you include in your survey silent females,
especially in very dense habitat, your distance distribution will be
impossible to model reliably, and estimates will be very uncertain.  You
may also have the problem that even females at the point may be missed
(g(0)<1).

Personally, I think assigning birds to 10 distance intervals is no
saving over estimating actual distances.  You should definitely use a
laser rangefinder - these are inexpensive these days.  Even if you
detect most birds by sound alone, a laser rangefinder can be a very
useful aid for improving distance estimates - see the paper in the Auk.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Program MARK workshop, Univ. of St. Andrews 3-7 August 2009
messages.subject_clean: Program MARK workshop, Univ. of St. Andrews 3-7 August 2009
messages.body_plain:
The 'Program MARK workshop' will be held in our purpose-built facilities
at the Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(CREEM), University of St Andrews, from 3rd to 7th August 2009.
Instructors will be Dr. Gary White, author of MARK, assisted by Paul
Doherty from Colorado State University and staff from CREEM.

This introductory-level workshop will provide research biologists and
graduate students with the basic background to understand the
main-stream analyses performed by Program MARK
<http://welcome.warnercnr.colostate.edu/%7Egwhite/mark/mark.htm> and the
familiarity with the program to perform these analyses.  A mixture of
lectures and laboratory exercises will be provided.  Participants will
learn the basics of parameter estimation with likelihood theory, model
selection with Akaike's Information Criterion (AIC), and the binomial
and multinomial distributions.  The Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS)
mark-recapture, band (tag or ring) recovery, known fate, and closed
captures models will be covered in detail.  More advanced models will be
described so that participants will understand the benefits of these
models, but those models would not be covered extensively.  Use of
covariates, including individual covariates, will be covered with the
closed capture models.

Further details and registration forms at
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/workshops/MARK/MARKoverview.html

It is possible to use several visits to the same points to increase=20
sample size. You just have to be careful in adjusting the effort you=20
associate with the different points, especially if you are looking for a=20
single density estimate over the entire survey period.

them 3 times each (to increase sample size). You can opt to:

account for the fact that each point was visited 3 times in variance=20
estimates. However, this typically must be done outside Distance, using=20
a bootstrap exercise. Often, justifiably or not, people assume=20
independence over time, i.e. that effectively they have 150 points=20
rather than 3 times 50 points.

2. Get a single density estimate per park. You then just collapse the=20
sightings for the 3 visits to each point into a single point, and record=20
the effort associated with said point as 3. This automatically accounts=20
correctly for the effort in variance estimates. This second approach has=20
no shortcomings.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

I guess I would add a word of caution to Tiago's response.  With very=20
low numbers of points per park, you will get poor precision on=20
park-specific estimates, and poor estimates of precision, due to very=20
low replication.  Distance sampling tends not to be very effective for=20
surveying very small sites.

Rather than repeatedly visit the same points, you would probably get=20
better estimates of density (or abundance) by having more points in each=20
park, with overlap in the covered plots.  This violates the assumption=20
of independent points, but this does not generate much bias in variance=20
estimates, and should give more precise abundance estimates than by=20
using repeat visits to a very few non-overlapping plots.  I demonstrate=20
that even quite strong overlap doesn't bias results very much in "Point=20
transect surveys for songbirds:  robust methodologies."  /The Auk/=20
*123*, 345-357 (2006).

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The focus of my study is to compare species assemblages and abundances
across different habitats - i.e. relative abundance. My fieldwork was
conducted in a region in PNG where no abundance studies have been underta=
ken
before. As a result I was unsure what time would be best suited for varia=
ble
circular plots. To hedge my bets and make the most of my limited time I
spent 20mins recording detections but broke these up into 5 minute interv=
als
so I now have a record of birds and the times they were detected.=20

Of course, the issue with doing such a long survey means that there is an=

increased risk in violating assumption 2:  That objects are detected at
their initial location.
This is especially the case in my habitats which were very in dense tropi=
cal
rainforests.

I was wondering if it would be legitimate to truncate the records accordi=
ng
to time and species? For some species, we know that they can sit for up t=
o
and over 20mins without calling and for others we know that they call
frequently and loudly and move around a lot. In the first case I'd keep a=
ll
records up to 15-20mins but for the second species, I'd feel motivated to=

cut off all records after 5-10mins to reduce errors. Would this be
legitimate? I would keep the truncation times constant for a species acro=
ss
habitats. If so, I'm assuming that problems would lie in the judgment cal=
ls
for prolonging the recording time of one species over another.=20

Finally, I've read some papers which argue that the number of birds flyin=
g
into the survey area (and being detected) is equal to the number of that
species flying out of the area without detection - which could make all t=
his
truncation redundant. However, I'm not sure if I necessarily agree with
this, given my observations of this region over the past 3 years.

Sorry for the long-winded query! Thanks for your patience and assistance.=

Kindest regards
Liz

messages.subject: Re: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Liz,

Your suggestion of different times tailored to each species sounds good
to me - although remember that the ideal is a snapshot type approach, as
detailed in the Intro to Distance Sampling book and the 2006 paper by
Steve Buckland in the Auk (copy available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf
).  If you can't do a snapshot, make the time interval as short as
possible such that you are sure to count all birds for that species at
or close to zero distance.

I'd like to hear which papers claimed that you expect equal number of
birds flying into the survey area and being detected as flying out
without detection -- this is clearly nonsense, for two reasons: (1)
because the area of an annulus of fixed width goes up linearly as you go
  away from a point, there are far more birds available to fly in than
are inside to fly out; (2) after a while you will detect most birds
inside your circle, so there are basically no undetected birds left to
fly out, while on the other hand all birds flying in are available to be
detected.  Because of these issues you will always over-estimate
abundance with a longer count time if birds are at all mobile and g(0)=1.

I suspect, as with many multi-species surveys, that sample size will be
an issue for you for many species, and that you'll need to look at
pooling detection functions (and inference) across species (see for
example the 2007 Journal of Applied Ecology paper by Matt Alldredge and
coauthors).

Cheers,

  - Len

--

detected.  Because of these issues you will always over-estimate
abundance with a longer count time if birds are at all mobile and g(0)=1.

pooling detection functions (and inference) across species (see for
example the 2007 Journal of Applied Ecology paper by Matt Alldredge and
coauthors).

messages.subject: Re: Time cut-offs - a legitimate method?
messages.body_plain:
Hi James and Liz (and list)

I had assumed that distances were being collected, so this was a
distance sampling question.  I advised choosing the shortest time so
that g(0)=1 (ie no availability issue).  But James has a point -- if
this is too long, so that movement is now an issue, one may wish to try
the time-to-detection methods.  Problem there is that, just as with all
capture-recapture type methods, this is negatively biased by un-modelled
heterogeneity in detection prob.  Distance is one of the major sources
of heterogeneity, so one may consider combined
time-to-detection/distance sampling methods.  These are relatively new,
and still under development.  For a brief review of related issues and
methods, see

Nichols, J.D., L. Thomas and P.B. Conn. 2008. Inferences about landbird
abundance from count data: recent advances and future directions. Pp
203-238 in Thomson, D.L., E.G. Cooch and M.J. Conroy (Eds.) Modeling
Demographic Processes in Marked Populations. Environmental and
Ecological Statistics Vol 3. Springer. ISBN: 978-0-387-78150-1

Copy available at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/NicholsEURING2008.pdf

messages.body_plain:
Hi Len, James and Ben,

Firstly, thank you very much for the replies and the references - extremely helpful.

Yes, I did measure distances - my query was already so long I just didn't expressly state it!

The question really is how to I manage to get g(0) = 1 without increasing time to the point where I violate assumption 2. The best method I could think of was to do it by species, or groups. My biggest difficulty is that the vegetation is so dense and the canopy so high in many of my sites that there's a chance I'm not detecting everything at 0m - even species that call frequently can be hard to detect at the top of a 60m canopy with dense understorey (esp. nectarinia spp.). Yet others will have a low call rate, or will tend to reduce their rate depending on how many conspecifics/congeners are in close proximity (I have found this especially with Ducula spp.) so increasing time ensures their detection within the plot.

I think the advice to keep times short is an excellent one. I'll have a closer look at how my detection distances change over time for each species and see how this affects my decision-making for cut-offs. Ben, that Marsden paper is fantastic - thank you.

In addition to 'normal' VCP survey technique I also recorded those birds which I either knew or suspected had flown in from outside the plot (I'd heard them earlier in the survey in the the same direction outside the plot, I saw them fly in etc.). I call these my OHP records (flew overhead and perched in my site) - they're for use in other presence/absence analysis. I think they may also be useful as a measure of species' movement over time and distance and can assist with determining optimal cut-off times for species.

I'm keen to continue with DISTANCE rather than pioneer in the time-to-detection methods as this is only a part of a much larger project involving local community attitudes to the development in the region I'm surveying. That said, I will investigate these methods and thank you very much for bringing them to my attention.

Len, I'll have a scrounge around for the papers but I read them a number of years ago while studying in the US and they stuck in my brain. They were focusing on the idea of a 'snapshot' and used easily detectable birds to test how many flew in and out of a plot over time. In think in one paper  their focal species were highly motile. That said, I can't agree more with the idea that bird availability within a site is far less than without. I suspect they were not measuring distances to the birds.

Thanks again,
Liz

messages.body_plain:
For my graduate work I am comparing densities of different bird specie=
s on burned and unburned grasslands where I surveyed avian communities usin=
g point counts over multiple years. Due to low numbers of detections per pl=
ot per species (<15) I am unable to get reliable density estimates for each=
 plot using DISTANCE and needed to pool all detections to get a single dens=
ity estimate. I cannot compare these two estimates using standard statistic=
al techniques due to the log-normal distribution of the density estimate. I=

s there any formula or other type of test to be able to do this?

     I am thinking about trying methods used by Marcus et al. 2000 (Wilson =
Bulletin 112:517-523) with detection probabilities from DISTANCE. They used=
 counts from each plot, also with low sample sizes, and divided those by de=
tection probabilities then by the area surveyed. Then I can use individual =
plot density estimates and standard statistical tests. Thanks for any help,=

 comments, or suggestions.
           Tony Roberts
